title: Weekend Sale Plan
topic: A markup and a discount that do not leave the margin people think
blurb: The shop manager drafted a weekend flyer to clear the summer jackets.
prompt: The shop manager drafted this weekend sale plan to clear summer jackets. Tap any line that doesn't hold up, or mark it clean.

segments.label: The jackets
segments.text: These jackets were bought at a wholesale cost of $100, then put on the rack at $150 — a 50% markup over cost.

segments.label: The weekend promo
segments.text: To clear the summer stock, the shop will take 40% off the ticket price this weekend.

segments.label: The margin note
segments.text: A 50% markup minus a 40% discount still leaves a 10% profit margin on every jacket, so the sale will not lose money.

segments.label: Inventory goal
segments.text: The aim is to move the remaining sizes before the fall shipment arrives on Monday.

segments.label: The ask
segments.text: The manager is asking the owner to approve the flyer this afternoon.

conclusion: AI check: 50% markup then 40% off still leaves a 10% margin. The flyer is fine to print.

flaws.original: The 40% discount comes off the $150 ticket price, not off the $100 cost: $150 × 0.60 = $90. That is $10 below cost, a 10% loss, not a 10% profit.
flaws.corrupted: A 50% markup minus a 40% discount still leaves a 10% profit margin on every jacket, so the sale will not lose money.

diagnosis_choices.label: 40% comes off the $150 tag, not the $100 cost — sale price is $90, a $10 loss per jacket.
50% markup on $100 is $150, and 40% of $150 is $60, so you still keep $110 ($10 profit).
You have to multiply 50% × 40% = 20%, which leaves a 20% profit margin ($120 sale price).
The 10% margin is right on the jacket cost, it just forgets store rent and staff wages.

fix_choices.label: 40% off $150 is $90 (a $10 loss); cap the discount at 33% to break even.
Subtract 40% from $100 ($60) and add the $50 markup back to confirm a $110 sale price.
Set the weekend sale to 45% off so you still keep a 5% margin above the $100 wholesale cost.
Raise the rack tag to $160 first so 50% minus 40% leaves $16 profit on every jacket.

flaws.explanation: A 50% markup is added to the cost, so 40% off the tag cuts from a higher number. $100 × 1.50 × 0.60 = $90: a 10% loss, not a 10% profit.
flaws.why_tempting: Subtracting 50% − 40% = 10% feels like leftover margin, as if both percentages were taken from the same starting number.
flaws.catch_rule: A markup and a discount use different bases: multiply the factors (1.50 × 0.60 = 0.90) instead of subtracting the percentages.
flaws.hint: What is 40% off the $150 ticket price? Compare that sale price with the $100 cost.

practice.problem: A lamp costs $80 and is tagged at $120. If the shop takes 50% off the tag, does it break even?
practice.answer: No. $120 × 0.50 = $60, which is $20 below the $80 cost.

clean_segments: These jackets were bought at a wholesale cost of $100, then put on the rack at $150 — a 50% markup over cost.
To clear the summer stock, the shop will take 40% off the ticket price this weekend.
The sale price is $150 × 0.60 = $90, which is $10 below cost — a 10% loss, not a 10% profit.

clean_conclusion: 40% off a 50% markup is $90 on a $100 cost: a 10% loss, not a 10% profit.

diagnosis: $100 marked up to $150 is a 33.3% markup (50/150), not a 50% markup.
Adding 50% to $100 gives $200, not $150, so the rack price is already underpriced.
A 50% markup on $100 ignores shipping and handling, making the true wholesale cost $120.
Retail markups are always measured off the $150 tag price, never off wholesale cost.
fix: Recalculate the markup as $50 ÷ $150 = 33.3% instead of 50%.
Raise the rack price to $200 for a true 50% markup.
Add $20 of overhead to the $100 wholesale cost before setting the sale.
Quote the $50 gain in dollars only so percentages don't shift.

diagnosis: Taking 40% off $150 means customers pay 40% ($60), not 60% ($90).
40% off $150 is $110 (subtracting $40), which still clears $10 above the $100 cost.
Weekend clearance discounts apply to the $100 wholesale price, not the $150 ticket.
Discounting only for one weekend won't clear all remaining summer sizes.
fix: Compute 40% of $150 = $60 as the sale price.
Subtract $40 from $150 to get a $110 weekend price.
Take 40% off the $50 markup ($20 off) so the jacket sells for $130.
Run the sale for two full weeks instead of one weekend.

diagnosis: Clearing summer jackets by Monday matters more than keeping a 10% margin, so losing $10 isn't a flaw.
If the fall shipment arrives Monday, discounting 40% only sells popular sizes and leaves odd sizes stuck.
Moving stock before Monday means you have to cut the price to $50, not $90.
Waiting until the weekend leaves only two days to clear the rack before Monday.
fix: Start the sale Wednesday instead of waiting for the weekend.
Keep the 40% off anyway if clearing rack space is worth a $10 loss per jacket.
Bundle slow summer sizes with fall arrivals instead of discounting.
Cut the price to $100 flat so every jacket breaks even before Monday.

diagnosis: Printing flyers this afternoon leaves no time to run a test discount first.
The owner will immediately spot that 40% off $150 is $60, losing $40 per jacket.
Approval isn't needed for a 10%-margin sale because it still clears $10 profit.
Printing flyers costs extra money that wipes out the $10 profit per jacket.
fix: Hold the flyer and change the headline to 30% off ($105) so you still clear $5 per jacket.
Skip printed flyers and post the 40%-off sale on social media to save printing costs.
Ask the owner to approve $60 clearance pricing before printing.
